## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
*   Nationwide, white Americans are the only group with an age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rate (315 per 100,000) that is lower than the crude rate (386). Adjusting for age brings the mortality rate for white Americans from the second-highest to the second-lowest.

*   Once adjusted for age, the highest COVID-19 mortality rates for white Americans are in Kentucky (466), Mississippi (466), Oklahoma (454), Tennessee (437) and West Virginia (411).
Note: Nationwide statistics are derived from CDC reporting at the national level and are not suppressed. State level statistics are suppressed by CDC when the number of deaths is between 1-9.
_Editors note: This is a re-launched version of our__original Color of Coronavirus project__, which ran from April 2020 through March 2021. That project was based on harvesting data from the COVID-19 statistics reported separately from each state. Since that time the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics has developed a more robust system of tracking__COVID-19 mortality__, based on death certificates. While not without some issues (especially a known undercounting of American Indian deaths, which we address below) this data set is even more comprehensive than was the case in our original reporting of these issues. Even as we regret that tracking COVID-19 deaths is still a relevant pursuit, we hope that you will find our work meaningful and helpful in addressing the pandemic and understanding its impacts. As always, we welcome your feedback and insights (info@apmresearchlab.org)._

## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### SOURCES
###### **Mortality Data**
*   For total counts and for calculating cumulative crude rates and age-adjusted rates: CDC/NCHS - Distribution of COVID-19 Deaths and Populations, by Jurisdiction, Age, and Race and Hispanic Origin.  
*   For counts over time and for crude rates over time, monthly/national: CDC/NCHS - Provisional COVID-19 Deaths: Distribution of Deaths by Race and Hispanic Origin.  
*   For counts over time and for crude rates over time quarterly/states: CDC/NCHS - AH Quarterly Excess Deaths by State, Sex, Age, and Race.  
 According to the CDC, about 91% of these deaths have COVID-19 indicated as the underlying cause of death, while for the other 9% COVID-19 is one of multiple causes of death.  
**Population Data**
Mid-Year 2020 U.S. Census Data accessed via CDC-WONDER
*   National populations by race, all ages combined.  
*   State-level populations by race, all ages combined.  
*   For age adjustment, national population by age groups: Non-Hispanic, Hispanic.  
*   For age adjustment, state populations by age groups: Non-Hispanic, Hispanic.
All calculations and subsequent analysis are by APM Research Lab and available on our GitHub.

## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### NOTES
###### **Racial and Ethnic Groups**
Our labels of each racial or ethnic group correspond as follows: *   Latino — Hispanic or Latino ethnicity of any race
*   Pacific Islander — Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander  
*   Indigenous — Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native  
*   White — Non-Hispanic white  
*   Black — Non-Hispanic Black or African American   
*   Asian — Non-Hispanic Asian   
*   More than one race — Non-Hispanic more than one race

## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### NOTES
###### As noted above, Indigenous American deaths are known to be underreported by 34%. According to the CDC, deaths are also known to be underreported for non-Hispanic API (3%) and for Hispanic decedents (3%).


## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### NOTES
###### Some CDC datasets include a "more than one race" racial category and some include an "other" category. We have included the data that indicates more than one race when available, for which there is also an overall population figure available as a denominator when calculating rates. No such denominator is available for calculating rates for the "other" category. The deaths listed in the "other" category constitute less than 1% of total reported deaths.


## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### NOTES
###### **Age-Adjusted Rates**
While there are many features of the novel coronavirus that are still unclear, this we know with certainty: The risk of dying from COVID-19 rises sharply with advanced age. According to the CDC, people 65-74 years old have 65 times the risk of dying from COVID-19 compared to people aged 18-29. That risk increases to 140 times higher for people in the 75-84 age bracket, and 340 times for people age 85 or older.   
Due to this steep age gradient to COVID-19 mortality, it is important to consider the varying age distributions of America's racial and ethnic groups. A higher share of white Americans are in the older age brackets than any other group. And even within the same race groups, the age distribution varies by location—with retirement destination states such as Florida having a much higher share of older adults within their white population, for example.
To remove the role of these age differences from COVID-19 mortality rates, we have also produced age-adjusted rates. There are two main categories of methods used to produce age-adjusted rates: direct and indirect standardization. The direct method uses the age distribution of COVID-19 deaths within a racial or ethnic group, while the indirect method takes the total number of COVID-19 deaths within a racial ethnic group and applies mortality rates by age group from the national level (all races) to the age distribution of that racial or ethnic group.
We have used the direct method where possible, but the direct method requires knowing the numbers of deaths for each age grouping for each race and, when calculating at the state level, for each state. For states with smaller populations, there are instances where not all of the age groupings reach the threshold of at least 10 to be released by CDC. For these suppressed groups/places, we have used the indirect method to calculate an age-adjusted rate.

## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### NOTES
###### **Age-Adjusted Rates**
To evaluate the accuracy of the indirectly age-adjusted rates, we compared direct and indirect rates where possible. Most indirect rates were within 5% of the direct rates. Some were up to 10% different and two were approaching 15% different. The higher errors tended to be for groups/places with lower numbers of COVID-19 deaths. For this reason, we chose to not calculate indirect rates for groups/places with fewer than 200 COVID-19 deaths. The indirect rates tended to be higher than the direct rates, but not universally.
All of these numbers are available for download on our GitHub, including an indication of whether the age-adjustment for a particular group/place has been directly or indirectly calculated.
What do the results of these calculations mean? The age-adjusted rates indicate that many younger Americans who are Black, Latino, Indigenous or Pacific Islanders are dying of COVID-19—driving their mortality rates far above that of white and Asian Americans. Despite their relative youthfulness (a protective factor against COVID), their death rates are elevated.
It is important to note that, while age-adjusted mortality rates help us remove the influence of age differences in racial groups to examine disparities in outcomes, they are not the actual mortality rates experienced by these groups.

## Deaths of despair strike women too
#### Awards and Recognition
"We Americans are reluctant to acknowledge that our economy serves the educated classes and penalizes the rest. "A remarkable new book."—John Harris, _The Guardian_

The authors argue that the capitalism that lifted countless people out of poverty is now destroying blue-collar America. They have solutions to make it work for all. They had better be right."—_New Scientist_

#### Awards and Recognition
"[Case and Deaton] dive into and weave the data through different demographic and clinical lenses — race, gender, age, social connectedness, work history, and the most important through-line: education. Thus Case and Deaton connect the dots, literally, in the many charts that explain what factors are driving the _Deaths of Despair_."—Jane Sarasohn-Kahn, _Health Populi Blog_
"The rise in premature deaths among working-class whites has become a national crisis, and the authors tie the problem to the weakening position of labor, the growing power of corporations, and to a health-care sector that redistributes working-class wages to the wealthy."—_Publishers Weekly_

"Refreshing . . . a careful, deep, and troubling look at the America that lies beyond the Ivy League."—James K. Galbraith, _Project Syndicate_

"The policies that the authors advocate not only would address deaths of despair, they would improve the health and welfare of the American people more generally."—David Canning, _Science_
"[a] hard-hitting study of US capitalism."—Andrew Robinson, _Nature_
"The authors add an important dimension to the growing body of research on the suffering of African Americans in the US; but their main argument is that it is the uneducated white working class that is now in “long-term and slowly unfolding” freefall."—Anne Nelson, _Times Literary Supplement_

"Complementing their candid prose with enlightening charts and graphs, Case and Deaton make the scale and immediacy of the problem crystal clear. This is an essential portrait of America in crisis."—_Publishers Weekly_
"_Deaths of Despair_ is designed to shine a light on a generational catastrophe that could—perhaps will—become a multigenerational disaster. It does this with chilling precision."—Mike Jakeman, _Strategy+Business_
"Through simple figures and clear prose, it presents a huge bodyof evidence from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s WONDER database and other sources that the arc of the white working class’s fate over the last two decades is long, but it bends toward nihilism and an early grave."—Gabriel Rossman, _Washington Examiner_
"Elaborately explained and well-presented. . . . Case and Deaton’s well-written and gloomy book was meant as a warning. Relentlessly fighting an infectious disease, the U.S. government seems to have treated it as a handbook."—Joakim Book, _American Institute for Economic Research_
"Well-researched, compassionate."—Susan Babbitt, _New York Journal of Books_
"Simply put, this is a terrific book. I suspect it will be on many people’s top 10 book lists of 2020. Although written before COVID-19, the book’s critique of the US approach to health care and inequality is remarkably prescient. In many ways, the opioid crisis Case and Deaton analyze is a microcosm of the anguish the world is experiencing today, and we would be remiss not to pay attention to their insights."—Kenneth Rogoff, _Finance & Development_
"A must-read for anyone attempting to objectively understand our collective American pain as well as those gaining from it."—Rahul Gupta, _Democracy_

# Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism
## Deaths of despair strike women too
#### Awards and Recognition
"Building on Case and Deaton’s extraordinarily influential research on the mortality resulting from the tragic opioid epidemic in the United States, this book examines three causes of death – drug overdose, suicide, and alcohol-related liver disease – that have risen rapidly since the mid-1990s. It is extraordinarily well written – sweeping yet succinct. And though it was published before the COVID-19 crisis, its critique of the US approach to health care and inequality is remarkably prescient."—Ken Rogoff, _Project Syndicate_
"I’ll offer my own endorsement from the [New York Times Notable] 100: _Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism_, by Anne Case and Angus Deaton. It covers arguably the single most alarming development in American life, one that helps explain the frustration pulsing through the country: In many communities, people are not living as long as their parents did."—David Leonhardt, _New York Times_
"[A] well-argued, important book."—Rosamund Urwin, _Sunday Times_
"Case and Deaton’s extraordinary research in this book is an important warning of the consequences this might have for people’s health and wellbeing and family and community life."—Economic Annals, _Jelena Žarković_
"This book will be an instant classic, applying high quality social science to an urgent national matter of life and death. In exploring the recent epidemic of 'deaths of despair,' the distinguished authors uncover an absorbing historical story that raises basic questions about the future of capitalism. It is hard to imagine a timelier—or in the end, more hopeful—book in this season of our national despair."—Robert D. Putnam, author of _Bowling Alone_ and _Our Kids_
"In the face of a government that failed to protect ordinary working-class Americans from the greed-fueled opioid epidemic and a media that was slow to notice the problem, Anne Case and Angus Deaton are true sentinels. _Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism_ is an urgent and clarion call to rethink pain, inequality, justice, and the business of being human in America. This book explains America to itself. I underlined damn near every sentence."—Beth Macy, author of _Dopesick: Dealers, Doctors, and the Drug Company That Addicted America_

Emanuel, University of Pennsylvania
"With stunning data analysis, close observation, and smoldering urgency, Case and Deaton show why mounting deaths of despair are not only a public health disaster but also an indictment of the metastasizing stratification that is undermining working-class America."—David Autor, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
"This book explains so many of today's headlines with clear writing, sharp storytelling, and an almost symphonic use of research in economics, public health, and history. "America is experiencing a catastrophe. Those without a college degree are not just being left behind; they are dying from deaths of despair. "Deaths of despair among US whites with low education cannot be attributed to lack of access to health care or ignorance of healthy lifestyles. # Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism
## Deaths of despair strike women too
#### Awards and Recognition
"We Americans are reluctant to acknowledge that our economy serves the educated classes and penalizes the rest. But that’s exactly the situation, and _Deaths of Despair_ shows how the immiseration of the less educated has resulted in the loss of hundreds of thousands of lives, even as the economy has thrived and the stock market has soared."—Atul Gawande, _New Yorker_
"A highly important book."—Arlie Russell Hochschild, _New York Times Book Review_
"This highly important book examines the pain and despair among white blue-collar workers and suggests that the hopelessness they are experiencing may eventually extend to the entire American work force."—_New York Times Editors’ Choice_
"Excellent."—_Joyce Carol Oates on Twitter_
"Gripping. . . . [Case and Deaton] do not merely rehearse decades of mortality and wage statistics. Rather, they seek to catalogue how an entire way of life first frayed and then fell apart over the past half-century, and the cruelty of an American meritocracy that heaps lavish rewards on the winners while increasingly leaving others to rot."—Joshua Chaffin, _Financial Times_
"A remarkable new book."—John Harris, _The Guardian_
"Disturbing. . . . . Case and Deaton do a great job making the case that something has gone grievously wrong."—Jim Zarroli, _NPR_
"I highly, highly recommend it."—Cardiff Garcia, _NPR Planet Money’s The Indicator_
"[A] remarkable and poignant book."—Dani Rodrik, _Project Syndicate_
"The system is broken and every bit of it needs fixing. This is a sobering – and essential – book."—Diane Coyle, _Enlightened Economist_
"Why economics really matters is illustrated in _Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism_. . . . ## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
*   Nationwide, white Americans are the only group with an age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rate (315 per 100,000) that is lower than the crude rate (386). Adjusting for age brings the mortality rate for white Americans from the second-highest to the second-lowest.

*   Once adjusted for age, the highest COVID-19 mortality rates for white Americans are in Kentucky (466), Mississippi (466), Oklahoma (454), Tennessee (437) and West Virginia (411).
Note: Nationwide statistics are derived from CDC reporting at the national level and are not suppressed. State level statistics are suppressed by CDC when the number of deaths is between 1-9.
_Editors note: This is a re-launched version of our__original Color of Coronavirus project__, which ran from April 2020 through March 2021. That project was based on harvesting data from the COVID-19 statistics reported separately from each state. Since that time the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics has developed a more robust system of tracking__COVID-19 mortality__, based on death certificates. While not without some issues (especially a known undercounting of American Indian deaths, which we address below) this data set is even more comprehensive than was the case in our original reporting of these issues. Even as we regret that tracking COVID-19 deaths is still a relevant pursuit, we hope that you will find our work meaningful and helpful in addressing the pandemic and understanding its impacts. As always, we welcome your feedback and insights (info@apmresearchlab.org)._

texts.36:
## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### NOTES
###### **Age-Adjusted Rates**
While there are many features of the novel coronavirus that are still unclear, this we know with certainty: The risk of dying from COVID-19 rises sharply with advanced age. According to the CDC, people 65-74 years old have 65 times the risk of dying from COVID-19 compared to people aged 18-29. That risk increases to 140 times higher for people in the 75-84 age bracket, and 340 times for people age 85 or older.   
Due to this steep age gradient to COVID-19 mortality, it is important to consider the varying age distributions of America's racial and ethnic groups. A higher share of white Americans are in the older age brackets than any other group. And even within the same race groups, the age distribution varies by location—with retirement destination states such as Florida having a much higher share of older adults within their white population, for example.
To remove the role of these age differences from COVID-19 mortality rates, we have also produced age-adjusted rates. There are two main categories of methods used to produce age-adjusted rates: direct and indirect standardization. The direct method uses the age distribution of COVID-19 deaths within a racial or ethnic group, while the indirect method takes the total number of COVID-19 deaths within a racial ethnic group and applies mortality rates by age group from the national level (all races) to the age distribution of that racial or ethnic group.
We have used the direct method where possible, but the direct method requires knowing the numbers of deaths for each age grouping for each race and, when calculating at the state level, for each state. For states with smaller populations, there are instances where not all of the age groupings reach the threshold of at least 10 to be released by CDC. For these suppressed groups/places, we have used the indirect method to calculate an age-adjusted rate.
texts.37:
## FOCUS ON WHITE AMERICANS
### Age-adjusted mortality rate
##### NOTES
###### **Age-Adjusted Rates**
To evaluate the accuracy of the indirectly age-adjusted rates, we compared direct and indirect rates where possible. Most indirect rates were within 5% of the direct rates. Some were up to 10% different and two were approaching 15% different. The higher errors tended to be for groups/places with lower numbers of COVID-19 deaths. For this reason, we chose to not calculate indirect rates for groups/places with fewer than 200 COVID-19 deaths. The indirect rates tended to be higher than the direct rates, but not universally.
All of these numbers are available for download on our GitHub, including an indication of whether the age-adjustment for a particular group/place has been directly or indirectly calculated.
What do the results of these calculations mean? The age-adjusted rates indicate that many younger Americans who are Black, Latino, Indigenous or Pacific Islanders are dying of COVID-19—driving their mortality rates far above that of white and Asian Americans. Despite their relative youthfulness (a protective factor against COVID), their death rates are elevated.
It is important to note that, while age-adjusted mortality rates help us remove the influence of age differences in racial groups to examine disparities in outcomes, they are not the actual mortality rates experienced by these groups.

Underlying cause of death is malignant neoplasms of breast (ICD-10 codes: C50). The Multiple Cause of Death data available on CDC WONDER are county-level national mortality and population data. Data are based on death certificates for U.S. residents. Each death certificate contains a single underlying cause of death, up to twenty additional multiple causes, and demographic data. The number of deaths, crude death rates and age-adjusted death rates can be obtained by place of residence (United States national, state, and county), age group, race, Hispanic ethnicity, sex, year and month of death, weekday of death, place of death, autopsy status, and underlying and multiple cause of death (4-digit ICD-10 codes, 113 selected causes of death, 130 selected causes of death for infants, injury causes, or drug / alcohol induced causes of death). Two archive datasets offer subsets of these data. For more information, refer to Multiple Cause of Death data description.

The Multiple Cause of Death data available on CDC WONDER are county-level national mortality and population data. Data are based on death certificates for U.S. residents. Each death certificate contains a single underlying cause of death, up to twenty additional multiple causes, and demographic data. The number of deaths, crude death rates and age-adjusted death rates can be obtained by place of residence (United States national, state, and county), age group, race, Hispanic ethnicity, sex, year and month of death, weekday of death, place of death, autopsy status, and underlying and multiple cause of death (4-digit ICD-10 codes, 113 selected causes of death, 130 selected causes of death for infants, injury causes, or drug / alcohol induced causes of death). Two archive datasets offer subsets of these data. For more information, refer to Multiple Cause of Death data description.

**How?** See "How do I organize my data?" for more information. **Hints:** 1. **About age-adjusted rates:** When age-adjusted rates are calculated, you cannot group the data by Age Group. 2. **About charts:** You cannot make charts when your data has more than two By-Variables. 3. **About maps:** To make a map, you must request data with a geographic location variable, such as State or County, as a "By-Variable." Then click the Map tab. * * * **Death Counts** The death counts in the data represent deaths that occurred in the 50 United States and the district of Columbia, for the legal place of residence of the decedent. See Mortality data for more information. **Notes:** Death counts are **suppressed** for statistics representing zero to nine (0-9) deaths. See Assurance of Confidentiality for more information. * * * **Crude Rates** Crude Rates are expressed as the number of deaths reported each calendar year per the factor you select. The default factor is per 100,000 population, reporting the death rate per 100,000 persons. Crude Rate = Count / Population * 100,000 See Frequently Asked Questions about Death Rates . **Hints:** * Rates calculated with population estimates are per 100,000 persons by default. However, infant mortality rates are calculated per 1,000 live births by default. See Additional Rate Options to select the factor for rate calculations. * Select the precision for rate calculations in the Other Options section. When the rate calculated for a small numerator (incidence count) is zero, you may increase the precision to reveal the rate by showing more numbers to the right of the decimal point. **Notes:** * Rates for small populations should be interpreted with caution. * Rates are suppressed for statistics representing zero to nine (0-9) deaths. Corresponding denominator population figures are also suppressed when the population represents fewer than 10 persons. See Assurance of Confidentiality for more information. * Rates are marked as "**unreliable**" when the death count is less than 20. *

# Underlying Cause of Death 1999-2020
Rates are marked as "**not applicable**" when the population denominator figure is unavailable, such as persons of "not stated" or unknown age or Hispanic origin. Rates and populations are also not available for specific categories for month and weekday of death, place of death, whether an autopsy was performed, or any subset of ages 85 and over. * Crude rates are helpful in determining the need for services for a given population, relative to another population, regardless of size. Crude rates are influenced by the underlying age distribution of the state's population. Even if two states have the same age-adjusted rates, the state with the relatively older population (as demonstrated by having a higher median age) will have higher crude rates because incidence or death rates for most cancers increase with increasing age. * The population estimates for the denominators of incidence rates are race-specific and sex-specific population estimates. The population estimates are aggregated from the most detailed level selected. For example, if you have requested data for the nation grouped by state and by county, then the populations are the county-level population estimates aggregated to the state and national summaries. See Population Denominator Data Sources below for more information. * The population for "Infant age groups" is the number of live births in the given time period. See Infant Mortality for more information. * * * **Age-Adjusted Rates** Age-adjusted death rates are weighted averages of the age-specific death rates, where the weights represent a fixed population by age. They are used to compare relative mortality risk among groups and over time. An age-adjusted rate represents the rate that would have existed had the age-specific rates of the particular year prevailed in a population whose age distribution was the same as that of the fixed population. Age-adjusted rates should be viewed as relative indexes rather than as direct or actual measures of mortality risk. The year "2000 U.S. standard" is the default population selection for the calculation of age-adjusted rates. However, you can select other standard populations, or select specific population criteria to determine the age distribution ratios. See Frequently Asked Questions about Death Rates for more information. The rates of almost all causes of death vary by age. Age adjustment is a technique for "removing" the effects of age from crude rates, so as to allow meaningful comparisons across populations with different underlying age structures.

## Introduction
About one in eight American women, and roughly one in 755 men, will be diagnosed with breast cancer in their lifetime. Excluding skin cancers, it is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women in the United States, and more than 4 million breast cancer survivors live in the U.S. today, including more than 54,000 Colorado women diagnosed with breast cancer since 2001.[[i]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn1) Breast cancer touches families and communities across Colorado. This year alone, the American Cancer Society projects that 5,210 Colorado women will be diagnosed with breast cancer and 710 will lose their lives to it.
Real progress has been made in the past few decades in diagnosis and treatment. The national breast cancer mortality rate has fallen 44% since 1989, and in Colorado, falling mortality rates since 1999 have saved an estimated 3,400 lives. Colorado also reports some of the most favorable cancer outcomes in the country.
For Breast Cancer Awareness Month, this report examines how often breast cancer occurs in Colorado compared with other states, how those rates have changed over time, what stage zero breast cancer is and how it is counted, how the disease affects men, how Colorado’s survival and mortality compare nationally, and what the disease costs patients, families, and the state.

## Key Findings
**Colorado’s overall breast cancer rates are near the national average, but its cancer outcomes are among the most favorable in the country.**
*   Colorado records 134.8 new invasive breast cancer cases and 18.8 deaths per 100,000 women, against 133 and 19 nationally.  
*   For women diagnosed from 2016 to 2022, Colorado’s five-year relative survival rate for female breast cancer was 93.7%, **eighth highest**among reporting states.
**Colorado is tied for the lowest breast cancer mortality rate in the nation for women under 50.**
*   Colorado’s rate is 2.6 deaths per 100,000 women under 50, tied for the lowest in the nation with Vermont, and it fell 2.4% per year from 2020 to 2024. The state’s rate for women under 65 is 7 deaths per 100,000, **third lowest in the nation**.  
*   For women 65 and older however, Colorado’s rate of 100.2 is 11% above the national rate of 90.2 and showed no statistically significant decline from 2020 to 2024, while the national rate fell 0.7% per year.
**Colorado’s breast cancer mortality rate has fallen 27% since 1999, sparing an estimated 3,400 lives, but progress has slowed.**
*   The rate dropped from 24.8 to 18 deaths per 100,000 women between 1999 and 2024. Had it stayed at its 1999 level, about 3,400 more Colorado women would have died of breast cancer from 2000 through 2024. Since 2008, the rate has declined 0.4% per year, one-third the national pace of 1.2%, and recent progress has been slower among women 65 and older.
**Diagnoses are rising, and 5,210 Colorado women are projected to be diagnosed in 2026.**

## Key Findings
*   The age-adjusted incidence rate increased about 0.7% per year from the mid-2000s through 2023 in Colorado and nationally, and faster among women under 50. As the number of Colorado women 65 and older is projected to grow nearly 30% by 2035, CSI projects about 5,500 to 6,100 diagnoses a year.
**Places with higher mammography rates generally have lower breast cancer mortality rates.**
*   In a CSI analysis of U.S. counties, the fifth with the highest mammography rates had a breast cancer mortality rate about 13% lower than the fifth with the lowest, and a smaller share of cancers diagnosed at a late stage. **Within Colorado, CDC estimates place 58 of 64 counties below the median U.S. county screening rate.**
**CSI estimates total spending on breast cancer care in Colorado at roughly $560 million a year, including about $62 million paid out of pocket by patients.**
*   In a 2022 study of insured patients, two-year health care costs averaged about $136,800 for those diagnosed at stage I, $267,500 at stage III and $501,200 at stage IV, in today’s dollars.

## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Colorado’s breast cancer incidence and overall mortality are both near the national average. From 2019 to 2023, Colorado recorded 134.8 new invasive breast cancer cases per 100,000 women, slightly above the U.S. rate of 133 and 23rd highest among the states. From 2020 to 2024, Colorado’s mortality rate of 18.8 per 100,000 women sat just below the national average of 19, and 21st lowest.[[ii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn2) That overall rate masks a sharp difference by age. Colorado’s rate for women under 65, 7 deaths per 100,000, is the third lowest in the nation, and its rate for women under 50, 2.6, is the lowest. For women 65 and older, Colorado’s rate of 100.2 per 100,000 is 11% above the national rate of 90.2 and among the 10 highest in the nation.
Because women 65 and older account for about 70% of Colorado’s breast cancer deaths, their higher rate pulls the state’s overall rate up to the national average.[[iii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn3) Colorado recorded 22,699 diagnoses during 2019–2023 and 3,301 deaths during 2020–2024, averaging about 4,500 diagnoses and 660 deaths annually over their respective periods.
Rates vary widely across the country. Delaware (148.1), Connecticut (147.4), and North Carolina (144.6) record the highest incidence.

## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Interestingly, the mountain west region has the three lowest rate states, although no clear reason can be attributed for this: Nevada (112.2), New Mexico (118.2), and Arizona (118.8). Massachusetts (15.2), Rhode Island (15.5), and Hawaii (16.1) post the lowest mortality rates; Mississippi (23.6), Oklahoma (22.3), and Delaware (22) have the highest.
Figure 1. Female breast cancer incidence (2019-2023) and mortality (2020-2024) by state, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 women. Source: CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026.
Colorado women compare favorably on several breast cancer risk factors, though these measures capture only part of breast cancer risk. In 2024, Colorado women had the lowest obesity rate in the nation, 26.2% against 34.4% nationally, and the second lowest rate of physical inactivity among the states, 16.9% against 24.2%. Among the risk factors examined here, Colorado compares less favorably on alcohol: in 2024, 14.4% of Colorado women reported binge drinking, above the national rate of 12.7%.[[iv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn4) The American Cancer Society attributes 16% of U.S. breast cancers to alcohol consumption.[[v]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn5) Screening also shapes the numbers: states that find cancer earlier record higher incidence, a pattern discussed later in this report.

## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Diagnoses are moving in the other direction. Colorado’s breast cancer incidence rate has increased about 0.7% per year since the mid-2000s (2004 in Colorado and 2005 nationally), the same pace as the nation. Nationally, the increase is steeper among younger women: from 2013 to 2022, incidence among women under 50 rose 1.4% per year, against 0.7% for women 50 and older.[[ix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn9) Colorado shows the same pattern: from 2019 to 2023, incidence among Colorado women under 50 rose 1% per year, while the trend among women 50 and older was not statistically significant.[[x]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn10) About one in five Colorado breast cancer diagnoses from 1999 to 2022 occurred in women under 50.[[xi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn11) The American Cancer Society identifies excess body weight, having fewer children, and having a first child after age 30 as possible contributors to the national rise among younger women. These are population-level associations and do not explain why any individual develops breast cancer.[[xii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn12)

## 2026 Estimates
The American Cancer Society projects 5,210 new female breast cancer cases and 710 breast cancer deaths in Colorado in 2026.[[xiii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn13) Breast cancer is projected to account for 17% of the state’s 30,160 new cancer cases and 8% of its 8,740 cancer deaths.
The 2026 projections exceed the highest annual counts observed in CDC data dating to 1999: 4,695 diagnoses and 684 deaths, both recorded in 2023. Since 1999, observed annual diagnoses have risen 64% through 2023 and deaths 34% through 2024.[[xiv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn14) Population growth and aging contribute to rising case counts, while the age-adjusted incidence rate has also increased. The American Cancer Society cautions that its projections are model-based and not suited to tracking trends, so the observed rates remain the best measure of progress.[[xv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn15) Colorado’s 2024 breast cancer mortality rate of 18 per 100,000 women was the second lowest on record, behind only 2019 (17.6).
Figure 3. Annual breast cancer diagnoses and deaths among Colorado women, 1999-2023. Diagnoses are new invasive cases and exclude stage zero; deaths are those with breast cancer as the underlying cause. Counts rise with population growth and aging as well as with changes in risk, so they increase faster than the age-adjusted rates discussed in this report.

## 2026 Estimates
If current trends hold, CSI projects Colorado’s 2026 breast cancer mortality rate at about 18.3 per 100,000 women, among the lowest on record and roughly 25% below 1999. The projection extends the joinpoint trend described above; Colorado’s annual rate typically varies by about one death per 100,000 women around that trend.
Colorado’s aging population will push case counts higher even if rates hold steady. The State Demography Office projects that the number of Colorado women 65 and older will grow 29% between 2023 and 2035, to about 662,000.[[xvi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn16) Applying current age-specific rates, CSI projects about 5,500 breast cancer diagnoses and 820 deaths a year in Colorado by 2035. If incidence keeps rising 0.7% per year and mortality keeps falling 0.4% per year, the 2035 totals would be about 6,100 diagnoses and 780 deaths. At today’s first-year cost per patient, care for women diagnosed in 2035 would cost at least $231 million in today’s dollars.
Nationally, the American Cancer Society projects 321,910 new invasive breast cancer cases among women, 60,730 cases of stage zero breast cancer and 42,140 deaths in 2026. About one in eight U.S. women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in her lifetime, and more than 4 million breast cancer survivors live in the United States.[[xvii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn17)

## Stage Zero Breast Cancer
Stage zero breast cancer, known as ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), is a growth of abnormal cells confined to the milk ducts that has not invaded surrounding breast tissue. Almost all cases are found through screening mammography.[[xviii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn18) About one in six breast cancer diagnoses nationally is stage zero: the American Cancer Society projects 60,730 stage zero cases in 2026 on top of 321,910 invasive cases, or 60,730 of 382,640 in total. Stage zero is not counted in the invasive incidence rates reported above.[[xix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn19) A 2015 study of women who received care after a DCIS diagnosis found that about 3% died from breast cancer within 20 years.[[xx]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn20)
Rising diagnoses are not only stage zero or early-stage cancers, however. National SEER data shows the rate of breast cancers first diagnosed after spreading to distant organs rose 33% between 2004 and 2023, from 6.4 to 8.5 per 100,000 women.[[xxi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn21) Advanced disease is not necessarily the result of missed screening: some cancers are not detected by a screening mammogram or develop between regular screenings, and some cancers first treated at an early stage return later.[[xxii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn22) Improving access to screening, timely diagnosis and effective treatment all offer opportunities for further progress.

## Introduction
About one in eight American women, and roughly one in 755 men, will be diagnosed with breast cancer in their lifetime. Excluding skin cancers, it is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women in the United States, and more than 4 million breast cancer survivors live in the U.S. today, including more than 54,000 Colorado women diagnosed with breast cancer since 2001.[[i]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn1) Breast cancer touches families and communities across Colorado. This year alone, the American Cancer Society projects that 5,210 Colorado women will be diagnosed with breast cancer and 710 will lose their lives to it.
Real progress has been made in the past few decades in diagnosis and treatment. The national breast cancer mortality rate has fallen 44% since 1989, and in Colorado, falling mortality rates since 1999 have saved an estimated 3,400 lives. Colorado also reports some of the most favorable cancer outcomes in the country.
For Breast Cancer Awareness Month, this report examines how often breast cancer occurs in Colorado compared with other states, how those rates have changed over time, what stage zero breast cancer is and how it is counted, how the disease affects men, how Colorado’s survival and mortality compare nationally, and what the disease costs patients, families, and the state.
texts.1:
## Key Findings
**Colorado’s overall breast cancer rates are near the national average, but its cancer outcomes are among the most favorable in the country.**
*   Colorado records 134.8 new invasive breast cancer cases and 18.8 deaths per 100,000 women, against 133 and 19 nationally.  
*   For women diagnosed from 2016 to 2022, Colorado’s five-year relative survival rate for female breast cancer was 93.7%, **eighth highest**among reporting states.
**Colorado is tied for the lowest breast cancer mortality rate in the nation for women under 50.**
*   Colorado’s rate is 2.6 deaths per 100,000 women under 50, tied for the lowest in the nation with Vermont, and it fell 2.4% per year from 2020 to 2024. The state’s rate for women under 65 is 7 deaths per 100,000, **third lowest in the nation**.  
*   For women 65 and older however, Colorado’s rate of 100.2 is 11% above the national rate of 90.2 and showed no statistically significant decline from 2020 to 2024, while the national rate fell 0.7% per year.
**Colorado’s breast cancer mortality rate has fallen 27% since 1999, sparing an estimated 3,400 lives, but progress has slowed.**
*   The rate dropped from 24.8 to 18 deaths per 100,000 women between 1999 and 2024. Had it stayed at its 1999 level, about 3,400 more Colorado women would have died of breast cancer from 2000 through 2024. Since 2008, the rate has declined 0.4% per year, one-third the national pace of 1.2%, and recent progress has been slower among women 65 and older.
**Diagnoses are rising, and 5,210 Colorado women are projected to be diagnosed in 2026.**
texts.2:
## Key Findings
*   The age-adjusted incidence rate increased about 0.7% per year from the mid-2000s through 2023 in Colorado and nationally, and faster among women under 50. As the number of Colorado women 65 and older is projected to grow nearly 30% by 2035, CSI projects about 5,500 to 6,100 diagnoses a year.
**Places with higher mammography rates generally have lower breast cancer mortality rates.**
*   In a CSI analysis of U.S. counties, the fifth with the highest mammography rates had a breast cancer mortality rate about 13% lower than the fifth with the lowest, and a smaller share of cancers diagnosed at a late stage. **Within Colorado, CDC estimates place 58 of 64 counties below the median U.S. county screening rate.**
**CSI estimates total spending on breast cancer care in Colorado at roughly $560 million a year, including about $62 million paid out of pocket by patients.**
*   In a 2022 study of insured patients, two-year health care costs averaged about $136,800 for those diagnosed at stage I, $267,500 at stage III and $501,200 at stage IV, in today’s dollars.
texts.3:
## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Colorado’s breast cancer incidence and overall mortality are both near the national average. From 2019 to 2023, Colorado recorded 134.8 new invasive breast cancer cases per 100,000 women, slightly above the U.S. rate of 133 and 23rd highest among the states. From 2020 to 2024, Colorado’s mortality rate of 18.8 per 100,000 women sat just below the national average of 19, and 21st lowest.[[ii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn2) That overall rate masks a sharp difference by age. Colorado’s rate for women under 65, 7 deaths per 100,000, is the third lowest in the nation, and its rate for women under 50, 2.6, is the lowest. For women 65 and older, Colorado’s rate of 100.2 per 100,000 is 11% above the national rate of 90.2 and among the 10 highest in the nation.
Because women 65 and older account for about 70% of Colorado’s breast cancer deaths, their higher rate pulls the state’s overall rate up to the national average.[[iii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn3) Colorado recorded 22,699 diagnoses during 2019–2023 and 3,301 deaths during 2020–2024, averaging about 4,500 diagnoses and 660 deaths annually over their respective periods.
Rates vary widely across the country. Delaware (148.1), Connecticut (147.4), and North Carolina (144.6) record the highest incidence.
texts.4:
## Breast Cancer Rates in Colorado
Interestingly, the mountain west region has the three lowest rate states, although no clear reason can be attributed for this: Nevada (112.2), New Mexico (118.2), and Arizona (118.8). Massachusetts (15.2), Rhode Island (15.5), and Hawaii (16.1) post the lowest mortality rates; Mississippi (23.6), Oklahoma (22.3), and Delaware (22) have the highest.
Figure 1. Female breast cancer incidence (2019-2023) and mortality (2020-2024) by state, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 women. Source: CDC/NCI U.S. Cancer Statistics, June 2026.
Colorado women compare favorably on several breast cancer risk factors, though these measures capture only part of breast cancer risk. In 2024, Colorado women had the lowest obesity rate in the nation, 26.2% against 34.4% nationally, and the second lowest rate of physical inactivity among the states, 16.9% against 24.2%. Among the risk factors examined here, Colorado compares less favorably on alcohol: in 2024, 14.4% of Colorado women reported binge drinking, above the national rate of 12.7%.[[iv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn4) The American Cancer Society attributes 16% of U.S. breast cancers to alcohol consumption.[[v]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn5) Screening also shapes the numbers: states that find cancer earlier record higher incidence, a pattern discussed later in this report.
texts.7:
## Breast Cancer Rates Over Time
Diagnoses are moving in the other direction. Colorado’s breast cancer incidence rate has increased about 0.7% per year since the mid-2000s (2004 in Colorado and 2005 nationally), the same pace as the nation. Nationally, the increase is steeper among younger women: from 2013 to 2022, incidence among women under 50 rose 1.4% per year, against 0.7% for women 50 and older.[[ix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn9) Colorado shows the same pattern: from 2019 to 2023, incidence among Colorado women under 50 rose 1% per year, while the trend among women 50 and older was not statistically significant.[[x]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn10) About one in five Colorado breast cancer diagnoses from 1999 to 2022 occurred in women under 50.[[xi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn11) The American Cancer Society identifies excess body weight, having fewer children, and having a first child after age 30 as possible contributors to the national rise among younger women. These are population-level associations and do not explain why any individual develops breast cancer.[[xii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn12)
texts.8:
## 2026 Estimates
The American Cancer Society projects 5,210 new female breast cancer cases and 710 breast cancer deaths in Colorado in 2026.[[xiii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn13) Breast cancer is projected to account for 17% of the state’s 30,160 new cancer cases and 8% of its 8,740 cancer deaths.
The 2026 projections exceed the highest annual counts observed in CDC data dating to 1999: 4,695 diagnoses and 684 deaths, both recorded in 2023. Since 1999, observed annual diagnoses have risen 64% through 2023 and deaths 34% through 2024.[[xiv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn14) Population growth and aging contribute to rising case counts, while the age-adjusted incidence rate has also increased. The American Cancer Society cautions that its projections are model-based and not suited to tracking trends, so the observed rates remain the best measure of progress.[[xv]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn15) Colorado’s 2024 breast cancer mortality rate of 18 per 100,000 women was the second lowest on record, behind only 2019 (17.6).
Figure 3. Annual breast cancer diagnoses and deaths among Colorado women, 1999-2023. Diagnoses are new invasive cases and exclude stage zero; deaths are those with breast cancer as the underlying cause. Counts rise with population growth and aging as well as with changes in risk, so they increase faster than the age-adjusted rates discussed in this report.
texts.9:
## 2026 Estimates
If current trends hold, CSI projects Colorado’s 2026 breast cancer mortality rate at about 18.3 per 100,000 women, among the lowest on record and roughly 25% below 1999. The projection extends the joinpoint trend described above; Colorado’s annual rate typically varies by about one death per 100,000 women around that trend.
Colorado’s aging population will push case counts higher even if rates hold steady. The State Demography Office projects that the number of Colorado women 65 and older will grow 29% between 2023 and 2035, to about 662,000.[[xvi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn16) Applying current age-specific rates, CSI projects about 5,500 breast cancer diagnoses and 820 deaths a year in Colorado by 2035. If incidence keeps rising 0.7% per year and mortality keeps falling 0.4% per year, the 2035 totals would be about 6,100 diagnoses and 780 deaths. At today’s first-year cost per patient, care for women diagnosed in 2035 would cost at least $231 million in today’s dollars.
Nationally, the American Cancer Society projects 321,910 new invasive breast cancer cases among women, 60,730 cases of stage zero breast cancer and 42,140 deaths in 2026. About one in eight U.S. women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in her lifetime, and more than 4 million breast cancer survivors live in the United States.[[xvii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn17)
texts.10:
## Stage Zero Breast Cancer
Stage zero breast cancer, known as ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), is a growth of abnormal cells confined to the milk ducts that has not invaded surrounding breast tissue. Almost all cases are found through screening mammography.[[xviii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn18) About one in six breast cancer diagnoses nationally is stage zero: the American Cancer Society projects 60,730 stage zero cases in 2026 on top of 321,910 invasive cases, or 60,730 of 382,640 in total. Stage zero is not counted in the invasive incidence rates reported above.[[xix]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn19) A 2015 study of women who received care after a DCIS diagnosis found that about 3% died from breast cancer within 20 years.[[xx]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn20)
Rising diagnoses are not only stage zero or early-stage cancers, however. National SEER data shows the rate of breast cancers first diagnosed after spreading to distant organs rose 33% between 2004 and 2023, from 6.4 to 8.5 per 100,000 women.[[xxi]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn21) Advanced disease is not necessarily the result of missed screening: some cancers are not detected by a screening mammogram or develop between regular screenings, and some cancers first treated at an early stage return later.[[xxii]](https://commonsenseinstituteus.org/research/breast-cancer-awareness-month-colorado-spotlight/#_edn22) Improving access to screening, timely diagnosis and effective treatment all offer opportunities for further progress.
